title: "You stole my purse"
notes: DRAFT for content-owner review. Same for everyone: no setup question and no variants. Every by-variant block has one 'default' entry and every *VariantMap is empty.
Placeholders as in quiz.json: {recipient}, {Recipient}, {possessive}, {Possessive}, {object}. The subject is always {recipient}, never {pronoun}.
Default example is a lost purse: a neutral everyday moment. Heavier accusations are not covered here.
Same three steps as lessons 1 and 2: notice the feeling, reassure, offer to help look.

steps.label: Notice the feeling
steps.example: It's upsetting when something goes missing.

steps.label: Reassure
steps.example: I'm here, and we'll find it.

steps.label: Offer to help look
steps.example: Shall we look together, starting in the bedroom?

default.setup: You're getting ready to go out. {Recipient} can't find {possessive} purse, looks around, and turns to you:
default.line: Someone took my purse. Was it you? You stole it.

screens.question: What would you say?

default.text: I didn't take it! Why would I steal your purse?
default.feedback: Almost everyone says this. It hurts to be accused, and defending yourself is natural. But it turns into an argument, and the purse is still missing.

default.text: Nobody took it. You just put it somewhere and forgot.
default.feedback: It's true, and you're trying to calm things. But "you forgot" can feel like blame, and the worry stays.

default.text: Let's look for it. It's probably in the bedroom.
default.feedback: Practical and kind. Looking together is a good move. It skips the feeling, and "probably" is a guess that may not work out.

default.text: It's upsetting when your purse is missing. I'm here, and we'll find it. Shall we look together, starting in the bedroom?
default.feedback: This names the feeling, reassures {object}, and offers to help look. You don't argue, and you don't accept the blame.

screens.afterChoice: You can try another answer to compare.

screens.title: The worry is real, even if the story isn't.
screens.body: When something is missing, the mind looks for a reason, and "someone took it" is an easy one. {Recipient} isn't trying to hurt you. The feeling of losing something important is real, and that's what you can answer.

options.label: Worry or fear
options.response: Often, yes. Losing something we need feels unsettling.

options.label: Anger at me
options.response: It can sound that way. Good instinct to take it seriously. Often it's the worry speaking, not a feeling about you.

options.label: Wanting a fight
options.response: It can feel like that in the moment. Usually it's a worried person looking for answers.

screens.title: Don't argue it. Join the search.
screens.body: Proving that nobody took it rarely helps, and it adds a second upset. Use the three steps instead: notice the feeling, reassure {object} that you're on {possessive} side, and offer to look together.

miniTask.question: Which reply follows all three steps?

options.label: I haven't touched your purse. Nobody has.
options.response: Understandable. But it defends you and skips the feeling.

options.label: That sounds upsetting. I'm here, and we'll find it. Shall we check the kitchen together?
options.response: Yes: feeling, reassurance, something to do together.

screens.title: Keep the search short and calm.
screens.body: Start with the usual spots: coat pockets, bags, drawers. Walk with {object} and keep your voice easy. Later, pick a "home" for important things, like a bowl by the door, and show {object} where it is. A spare key helps too.

screens.title: Being accused hurts. Take a moment first.
screens.body: It's normal to feel stung, even when you know it's the worry talking. A small pause before you answer helps you stay kind.

miniTask.question: Pick your pause for next time:

options.label: One slow breath before I answer
Tell myself: this is the worry talking
Step away for a minute, if it's safe

screens.title: Practice: a missing purse
screens.intro: Now try it out loud. {Recipient} is an AI practice partner. Type what you'd say. The coach will show what worked.

default.stage: After a few minutes of looking.

You took it, didn't you? I want it back.

fallbackScenarios.setup: You're getting ready to go out. {Recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: I can't find my purse. Did you move it?

answers.text: No, I didn't touch it. You must have put it somewhere.
answers.feedback: It's true, but it can sound like blame.

answers.text: Losing your purse is stressful. I'm here. Shall we look together, starting by the door?
answers.feedback: Feeling, reassurance, and a search together.

answers.text: I'll help you look for it.
answers.feedback: A good offer. Naming the feeling too would make it warmer.

fallbackScenarios.setup: After a few minutes of looking, {recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: Somebody took it. I know somebody took it.

answers.feedback: Kind and honest, but it doesn't touch the worry.

answers.text: Nobody took it! It's here somewhere!
answers.feedback: Almost everyone feels this. But raising your voice adds to the upset.

answers.text: You're really worried about it. I'm with you, and we'll keep looking. Want to check your coat pockets?
answers.feedback: You named the worry, stayed on {possessive} side, and gave one small step.

fallbackScenarios.setup: Later, back in the kitchen, {recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: You took it, didn't you? I want it back.

answers.text: I'm not a thief. How can you say that?
answers.feedback: It hurts to hear. Stepping back from the blame, even silently, helps you stay calm.

answers.text: I can hear how much you want it back. I'm here, and we'll find it. Shall we have a look in the bedroom?
answers.feedback: You didn't argue or accept blame. You gave the feeling a place to go.

answers.text: I don't have it. Let's keep looking.
answers.feedback: Calm and honest. A word about the feeling would make it warmer.

default.question: Did {recipient} look for something that felt lost or taken since yesterday?

options.label: Not yet
options.response: Your plan is ready for when it does.

options.label: It helped
options.response: That's real progress. Looking together is a strong way to calm things.

options.label: Partly
options.response: That's normal at first. Keep the same calm words for a few days. Familiar words help.

options.label: It didn't help
options.response: That happens. Here are a few more ways to try.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Look first, talk second
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Start walking toward the usual spots, and say one calm sentence along the way. Moving together can settle a worry faster than words.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Give things a home
followUpsDidntHelp.text: A bowl by the door for keys and a hook for the purse make the search shorter, and the worry smaller.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Keep a spare
followUpsDidntHelp.text: A second set of keys, or a copy of a favorite card, lowers the stakes of losing the first.

doctorNote.text: If the worry about things being taken is new or growing, mention it at the next doctor visit.

default.stage: Morning. You're about to leave the house.
default.line: Where are my keys? Somebody moved them.
Nobody ever puts things back where they were.
